reflection_question: What is one thing you already know God wants you to do that you have not done yet?
devotional_text:
Imagine God tells you to build something you have never built, for a disaster you cannot see yet. No storm clouds. No warning on the news. No neighbor building one next door. Just a word from God and a set of measurements. That is where Noah is standing. Last time we read, the whole world had gone bad. Every imagination of the heart was only evil continually. And then came one small word. But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD. Now we finally meet the man. Who is Noah? What kind of life does a man live in a world like that, where violence is everywhere and nobody seems to care? And what exactly does God tell him to do? Because grace was not the end of Noah’s story. It was the start of a lot of work. Trees had to come down. Rooms had to be built. Pitch had to be spread. Food had to be gathered for a boat full of people and animals. God gave the word. Noah built the boat. Today we are reading Genesis 6:9–22.

T H U S D I D N O A H “These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with God.” G E N E S I S 6 : 9 There is that heading again. These are the generations of. We saw it with the heavens and the earth. We saw it with Adam’s family. Now Genesis opens a new part of the story, and this part belongs to Noah. Three things are said about him. He was just. That means righteous. A man who did what was right. He was perfect in his generations. That does not mean Noah never sinned. It means he was a man of integrity, blameless among the people of his time. In a crooked world, he was straight. And the third one. Noah walked with God. Where have we heard that before? Enoch, Noah’s great grandfather. Genesis 5 said Enoch walked with God. Now Noah does the same thing. The walk got passed down. Then we hear about his family. Noah begat three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. We met them at the end of Genesis 5. They each have a wife, and every one of them is going to matter in this story. Now look at the world Noah lives in: “The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. And God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 1 – 1 2 Corrupt means ruined. Spoiled. Rotten. Like fruit that has gone bad all the way through. And all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth. Everybody had wandered off the road God made.

Then the word violence. The earth was filled with it. Think about where this started. Cain killed Abel in a field. Lamech killed a man and bragged about it. Back then it was one murder, then another. Now the whole earth is filled. Violence has become the normal language of the world. This is why judgment is coming. God is not angry over nothing. People are hurting people. Everywhere. All the time. The ones made in God’s image are destroying each other. “And God said unto Noah, The end of all flesh is come before me; for the earth is filled with violence through them; and, behold, I will destroy them with the earth.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 3 God tells Noah exactly what He is going to do. He does not keep him in the dark. And then, right away, He gives him a job: “Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 4 An ark is a big vessel built to keep something safe. It is not a sailboat with a steering wheel. Think of a giant floating box, made to carry life through the storm. Gopher wood is the name of the wood. It has nothing to do with the little animal. It is a Hebrew word for a kind of timber, and the exact tree is not certain today. What matters is that God picked the material. Rooms means compartments. Separate spaces inside. And pitch is a thick, sticky, tar like coating used to seal wood so water cannot get in. Noah was to cover the ark with it inside and outside.

“And this is the fashion which thou shalt make it of: The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 5 Fashion here means the design. The pattern. And a cubit was an ancient way to measure. It was the length of a man’s forearm, from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. It varied a little from place to place. Using about 18 inches for a cubit, the ark comes out to roughly 450 feet long, 75 feet wide and 45 feet high. That is about 137 meters long, 23 meters wide and 14 meters high. These are close numbers, not a modern blueprint. But they give you the picture. Lay it on the ground, and it stretches about one and a half football fields. This was not a little boat in a backyard. This was a massive building project. “A window shalt thou make to the ark, and in a cubit shalt thou finish it above; and the door of the ark shalt thou set in the side thereof; with lower, second, and third stories shalt thou make it.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 6 The window here is an opening near the top for light and air, finished a cubit from the roof. One door, set in the side. And three stories, which means three decks. Three floors. Look how detailed God is. He does not say, build something that floats. He gives the material, the sealing, the size, the light, the door and the floors. When God asks Noah to do something, He is not vague. He thought it through. Think about what each of those details is for. The pitch keeps the water out. The rooms keep living things in their places. The window lets in light and air. The door lets them in and will one day let them out. Every detail is about keeping life alive. God was planning for survival before a single drop fell.

But notice who has to swing the hammer. God gives the plan. Noah does the work. God does not snap His fingers and make an ark appear. Trees had to be cut down. Boards had to be shaped. Pitch had to be gathered and spread, coat after coat. This took a long time and a lot of sweat. “And, behold, I, even I, do bring a flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh, wherein is the breath of life, from under heaven; and every thing that is in the earth shall die.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 7 I, even I. God says it twice. Nobody else is behind this flood. God Himself is bringing it. And it will be complete. Everything with the breath of life under heaven will die. And then, right after that, comes the promise: “But with thee will I establish my covenant; and thou shalt come into the ark, thou, and thy sons, and thy wife, and thy sons’ wives with thee.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 8 Another but. Just like verse 8. Judgment for the world. But with thee. This is the first time the word covenant shows up in the Bible. A covenant is a solemn, binding commitment. Not a suggestion. Not friendly advice. A promise God ties Himself to. And notice, God calls it my covenant. He is the One making it, and He is the One who will keep it. There is more to this covenant still ahead, after the water is gone. But it starts right here. Look who is inside it. Noah. His wife. His three sons. And their three wives. Eight people. The New Testament counts them too:

“Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.” 1 P E T E R 3 : 2 0 Longsuffering means patience that holds out a long time. God waited while the ark was being built. And at the end, eight people out of the whole world. “And of every living thing of all flesh, two of every sort shalt thou bring into the ark, to keep them alive with thee; they shall be male and female. Of fowls after their kind, and of cattle after their kind, of every creeping thing of the earth after his kind, two of every sort shall come unto thee, to keep them alive.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 9 – 2 0 God is not only saving people. He is saving life. Birds. Cattle. Creeping things. Two of every sort, male and female, so life can start again when the water goes down. Here God gives the basic plan in pairs. Soon He will add more detail for certain animals. Kind is the word the story uses for groups of living things. It is the same word from creation, when God made every creature after his kind. It is not a modern science list of every species. It is the story telling us every family of living things would be kept alive. And notice, Noah does not have to chase them all down. The verse says they shall come unto thee. God brings them to him. “And take thou unto thee of all food that is eaten, and thou shalt gather it to thee; and it shall be for food for thee, and for them.” G E N E S I S 6 : 2 1

Even this. Food for eight people and every one of those animals, for as long as they would be inside. Somebody had to gather it, store it and plan it. God’s rescue came with real chores. Saving life meant caring for life. And then the verse the whole reading has been building toward: “Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he.” G E N E S I S 6 : 2 2 Thus did Noah. Not some of it. Not the parts that made sense to him. Not the parts that were easy. according to all that God commanded him, so did he. Think back over this book. Adam and Eve knew exactly what God said about the tree, and they did not do it. Cain heard God warn him that sin was lying at the door, and he did not listen. Knowing God’s words was never the problem. Doing them was. Noah heard, and Noah did. Hebrews tells us what was going on inside Noah while he built: “By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.” H E B R E W S 1 1 : 7 Things not seen as yet. That is the key. Noah was building for something he could not see. No flood yet. Just God’s word. And moved with fear means he took God seriously. Holy respect. He believed God meant what He said. That is faith. Not a feeling. A hammer in your hand because God said so. And look at the end of that verse. by the which he condemned the world. Every board Noah nailed was a message. The same world that did whatever it wanted could see one man doing what God said. His obedience made their rebellion

plain. He became heir of the righteousness which is by faith. Heir means the one who receives an inheritance. Noah did not earn God’s favor by building. He had already found grace. The building was how he answered it. Most of us will never be asked to build an ark. But most of us already know something God has told us to do. Forgive that person. Read His word. Love your family. Work honestly. Stay faithful when nothing seems to change. We do not see the results yet. That is exactly when obedience counts. The ark is built. The food is stored. Everything God said, Noah did. Now all that is left is for God to speak again and say come in.

reflection_question: Is there something you have been preparing for a long time but have not actually stepped into yet?
devotional_text:
The ark is finished. For years Noah has been building. Cutting the wood. Sealing it with pitch. Following every measurement God gave him. On our last day we closed with one simple line: Noah did everything God commanded him. But here is something to think about. A finished boat sitting on dry ground has not saved anybody yet. You can build something for years and never step inside it. You can plan, prepare, talk about it, and still stay right where you are. Building is one thing. Going in is another thing. So God speaks again. This time He is not handing Noah a blueprint. He is giving him an invitation. Come in. And then God adds something that might surprise you. He gives a date. Seven more days. One week left of normal life. One week where the sky is clear, the ground is dry, and the world outside looks exactly the same as it did yesterday. What do you do when you have obeyed God and nothing has happened yet? Do you keep going? Do you start to wonder if you heard Him right? Today we are reading Genesis 7:1–10.

F R O M B U I L D I N G T O E N T E R I N G Genesis 7 opens with God speaking. Not Noah. Not his family. God. “And the LORD said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation.” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 Look at the first word God uses. Come. He does not say go. He says come. That is the language of somebody who is already inside, waving you in. Noah is not being shipped off alone. He is being called into the place God prepared for him. And he is not coming alone. God says all thy house. Your house here does not mean the building. It means the household. The people who live under your roof and belong to your family. Who is that? God already told us back in Genesis 6:18: thou, and thy sons, and thy wife, and thy sons’ wives with thee. So it is Noah, his wife, his three sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and the wives of those three sons. Eight people. That is the whole list. Out of an entire world full of people, eight walk into that boat. Now look at why God says this. For thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation. To be righteous means to be right with God. Living in line with Him. Walking the way He walks. And notice where Noah is righteous. In this generation. That means among the people of his own time. The same people we read about on Day 14, when the earth was filled with violence and every thought of man’s heart was evil. Noah was not righteous in an easy place. He was righteous in the worst crowd the world has ever seen. But do not skip the order. Before the Bible ever called Noah just, it said this: Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD. Grace came first. Noah’s righteous life grew out of a God who looked at him with favor first.

And here is something worth seeing. Noah’s wife and sons and their wives come in with him. Noah was the one God spoke to. But the people under his roof were the ones who walked through that door beside him. Hebrews says he prepared an ark to the saving of his house. That was God’s word to Noah, in his moment. It is not a rule that every family is saved because one person in it believes. But it does show us that Noah’s obedience was never only about Noah. The people around him were affected by whether he listened to God or not. “Of every clean beast thou shalt take to thee by sevens, the male and his female: and of beasts that are not clean by two, the male and his female. Of fowls also of the air by sevens, the male and the female; to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth.” G E N E S I S 7 : 2 – 3 This is where the picture most of us grew up with gets bigger. The children’s version says the animals came two by two. That is true. Verse 9 says it. But it is not the whole story. God splits the animals into two groups. Clean beasts and beasts that are not clean. Clean here does not mean washed. It is not about mud. A clean animal is one God counted fit to be offered to Him. The other animals were not bad animals. They just were not set apart for that use. Later, in the law God gave Moses, He would spell out the clean and unclean animals in detail. But look at this. Noah lives long before Moses, and God does not stop to explain which is which. Noah already knows. God had been teaching people how to approach Him long before any of it was written down. For the clean animals and the birds, God says by sevens, the male and his female. Most people read this as seven pairs. Seven males and seven females. Many translations put it that way. Either way, the point is clear. There are a lot more clean animals than unclean ones.

Why? Jump ahead to the end of the flood: “And Noah builded an altar unto the LORD; and took of every clean beast, and of every clean fowl, and offered burnt offerings on the altar.” G E N E S I S 8 : 2 0 Think about that. If Noah only had two of each clean animal, offering one to God would wipe that kind of animal off the earth. The extra clean animals meant Noah could worship God on the other side and the animals could still keep going. And it was not for food. Not yet. Back on Day 4 we noticed that God gave mankind plants to eat. The permission to eat animals does not come until Genesis 9:3, after the flood. So these extra animals were not a pantry. They were for worship and for life. Now look at the reason God gives. To keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth. Seed means offspring. The next generation. The babies that come after. Go back to creation. God told the birds and the sea creatures to be fruitful and multiply. He made plants with seed in them. He built a world designed to keep going. Now that world is about to be judged, and God is protecting its future. The animals are not decoration on the ark. They are part of the rescue. “For yet seven days, and I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights; and every living substance that I have made will I destroy from off the face of the earth.” G E N E S I S 7 : 4 Yet seven days means seven more days. God puts a date on it. One week, and then rain for forty days and forty nights.

Living substance is an old way of saying every living thing. Every creature that has life in it. And notice how God describes them. That I have made. The One who judges the world is the same One who made it. He is not tearing down something that belongs to somebody else. So how does Noah respond to a warning like that? “And Noah did according unto all that the LORD commanded him.” G E N E S I S 7 : 5 We have heard almost these exact words before. At the end of chapter 6, after the building instructions, it said Noah did according to all that God commanded him. Now it says it again. That matters. Obeying once is not the same as being an obedient person. Noah obeyed when the job was building. Now the job is different. Leave your home. Gather your family. Get inside. And he obeys again. Same Noah. New situation. Same answer. “And Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters was upon the earth.” G E N E S I S 7 : 6 Six hundred years old. That is his age when the flood came, not when he started building. Earlier in Genesis 5 we read that he was five hundred when his sons were born. Noah is not a young man rushing into an adventure. He has a long life behind him on that land. “And Noah went in, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons’ wives with him, into the ark, because of the waters of the flood.” G E N E S I S 7 : 7

Because of the waters of the flood. Noah went in because God said the water was coming. Not because he could see it. He trusted the warning before there was anything to look at. Picture what that might have meant. Walking away from the house you lived in. The fields you knew. The roads you walked. Everything familiar, left on the other side of a wooden wall. And still they went. “There went in two and two unto Noah into the ark, the male and the female, as God had commanded Noah.” G E N E S I S 7 : 9 Look closely. There went in two and two unto Noah. The animals came to Noah. God had already said in chapter 6 that they would come to him. Noah did not have to chase down every creature on the earth. He built the boat. God brought the animals. And two and two describes how they came in. In pairs, male and female. It does not cancel out the sevens God just talked about. The clean animals came in pairs too. There were just more pairs of them. “And it came to pass after seven days, that the waters of the flood were upon the earth.” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 0 And there it is. Seven days, just like God said. Not six. Not eight. When the week was over, the water came. But think about that week. The ark was finished. The animals were there. The warning was given. And for seven days, nothing happened. The sun came up. The sun went down. The neighbors kept living their lives. That is a hard place to stand. You did what God said. You are ready. And everything outside still looks the same.

That is not a sign God forgot. It is not a sign Noah got it wrong. Sometimes obedience comes first and the visible change comes later. God’s warning and Noah’s action belonged together, even in the days when the sky gave no proof. Noah’s story does not promise that every week of waiting ends in something dramatic. But it does show us what a faithful person does while waiting. He keeps doing what God said. He stays ready. Building the ark took years. Walking in took one step. Noah had done the long obedience. Now he did the short one too, and he did it before a single drop fell.

reflection_question: Why do you think Genesis tells us that the LORD shut the door instead of Noah?
devotional_text:
Seven days of blue sky. And then it happened. God had warned about this for a long time. Noah had built for years. The animals had come. The family had gone in. Everything God said would happen was now about to happen. This is the part of the story most of us have seen painted on nursery walls. A cute boat. Smiling giraffes poking their heads out. A rainbow in the corner. But that is not what Genesis 7 describes. Genesis 7 describes the end of a world. Water bursting up from below. Water pouring down from above. Hills disappearing. Mountains disappearing. And every living thing outside one wooden boat, gone. It is hard to read. It should be hard to read. This is what judgment looks like when God has warned and warned and the world would not turn back. But inside the same chapter there is another picture. A door. A family. A boat lifted up by the very water that is destroying everything else. The same flood that judged the world carried Noah. Today we are reading Genesis 7:11–24.

T H E D A Y T H E W O R L D W A S U N D O N E Genesis does not start this part with a feeling. It starts with a date. “In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 1 Look how specific that is. Noah’s six hundredth year. The second month. The seventeenth day. This is not a vague old legend. The Bible marks the day like an entry in a logbook. Keep that date in your mind. Second month, seventeenth day. We are going to need it when the water starts going down. Now look at where the water comes from. Two places. The fountains of the great deep broken up. The great deep is the water below. The deep waters under the earth and the seas. Broken up means burst open. Water rising up from beneath. The windows of heaven were opened. The windows of heaven is a picture of the sky being opened. Water pouring down from above. Not a drizzle. The sky letting go. Water from below and water from above, at the same time. Genesis does not stop to explain the science of how. It tells us what happened and who caused it. Now go back to Day 2. God put a firmament in the middle of the waters and divided the waters above from the waters below. Then He gathered the waters together so the dry land could appear. That is how God made a world people could live on.

Look at what happens here. The water above comes down. The water below comes up. The line God drew between them is being erased. It is like watching creation run backward. The world God shaped out of the water is being swallowed by the water again. “And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights.” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 2 Forty days and forty nights, just like God told Noah. Every word of the warning is coming true on schedule. “In the selfsame day entered Noah, and Shem, and Ham, and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and Noah’s wife, and the three wives of his sons with them, into the ark;” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 3 Selfsame means that very same day. The day the fountains burst, the family was inside. Verses 13 to 16 go back over the entry we read on our last day, but with more detail. This is not a second group of people showing up. It is not a second flood. Genesis is slowing the camera down and showing us the moment again, closer up. And the sons are named again: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Eight people. Noah, his wife, his three sons, and their three wives. “They, and every beast after his kind, and all the cattle after their kind, and every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind, and every fowl after his kind, every bird of every sort.” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 4

After his kind. That phrase should sound familiar. It is creation language. On Day 3 we read it over and over as God filled the world with life. Every kind God made is represented inside that boat. The God who made each kind is now keeping each kind. “And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in.” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 6 Stop on that last line. And the LORD shut him in. Noah did not close the door. God did. Think about what that means. Noah’s safety did not depend on Noah getting the latch right. God Himself sealed him inside. The protection was God’s work, not Noah’s. But that same closed door means something else too. The door was open for a long time. Years of building. Seven days of waiting. And now it is closed, and it is God who closed it. The time to come in was over. Genesis does not linger outside that door, and it does not need to. On one side of that door, life. On the other side, judgment. And God is the one who decided where the door was. “And the flood was forty days upon the earth; and the waters increased, and bare up the ark, and it was lift up above the earth.” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 7 Bare up the ark means the water carried it. Lifted it. Look at that. The very water that was destroying the world was holding Noah up. The thing that meant death for everyone outside was the thing that floated the boat for everyone inside.

“And the waters prevailed, and were increased greatly upon the earth; and the ark went upon the face of the waters. And the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth; and all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered.” G E N E S I S 7 : 1 8 – 1 9 Prevailed means the waters won. They overpowered everything. And Genesis keeps turning the volume up. The waters prevailed. They prevailed greatly. They prevailed exceedingly. This is not a bad storm in one valley. Genesis paints it as huge. All the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered. That is the way the Bible tells it, and we should let it say what it says. “Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered.” G E N E S I S 7 : 2 0 Remember from Day 15, a cubit is about eighteen inches. Fifteen cubits is about twenty two feet. The water rose that far up over the high places. The mountains, the places people would run to when water rises, were underneath. Then comes the hardest part of the chapter. “And all flesh died that moved upon the earth, both of fowl, and of cattle, and of beast, and of every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth, and every man: All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died.” G E N E S I S 7 : 2 1 – 2 2 The breath of life. Remember Day 6. God formed man from the dust and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. That breath was God’s gift. And now the breath of life is going out of every nostril on dry land.

This is not the first death in the Bible. Abel died at his brother’s hand. Genesis 5 repeated and he died again and again. Death came into the world back in the garden. But this is death on a scale the world had never seen. And we should not rush past it. Animals died. Birds died. People died. Men, women, families. Genesis does not celebrate it. It just tells us, plainly and heavily, what the cost of a world full of violence turned out to be. Go back to Day 15 for a moment. God looked at the earth and saw it was corrupt and filled with violence. People were destroying each other. And God said He would destroy them with the earth. The flood is not God losing His temper on a good world. It is God judging a world that had already been tearing itself apart. Think about how the story got here. A bite of fruit God said not to eat. Then a brother killing a brother. Then Lamech bragging about killing a man. Then a whole earth full of violence. Sin did not stay small. It spread from one heart to one family to the whole world. And Genesis 7 is where that road ends. That is why this chapter matters. Sin is never as small as it looks when it starts. “And every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground, both man, and cattle, and the creeping things, and the fowl of the heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth: and Noah only remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark.” G E N E S I S 7 : 2 3 And Noah only remained alive. After a list of everything that was lost, one small line. Noah, and those with him. Eight people and the animals God brought. That is all that was left. Jesus Himself pointed back to this moment:

“For as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark, And knew not until the flood came, and took them all away; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.” M A T T H E W 2 4 : 3 8 – 3 9 Noe is just the Greek way of saying Noah. And look at what Jesus says the people were doing. Eating. Drinking. Getting married. Normal life. They were not ready because they did not take the warning seriously. Jesus says the same will be true when He comes back. The lesson is not to point at disasters and blame people. The lesson is to take God’s warning seriously yourself. “And the waters prevailed upon the earth an hundred and fifty days.” G E N E S I S 7 : 2 4 Now let us get the timeline straight, because it is easy to get wrong. Most of us picture Noah in the ark for forty days. That is not what Genesis says. The rain fell for forty days and forty nights. But the waters prevailed for a hundred and fifty days. And those forty days of rain are inside the hundred and fifty, not added on top. So the rain stopped, but the water did not go away. For the rest of those hundred and fifty days, it still covered everything. Why does Genesis give us all these numbers? Because this was not a bad night. It was a long season. Real people lived through every one of those days, one sunrise at a time, with water in every direction. That is five months of nothing but water. Noah was saved. But being saved was not the same as being finished. He was alive in a world he could not step back into yet.

So the chapter ends without an ending. The waters are still up. The ark is still floating. The door is still shut. Everything outside is gone, and everything inside is waiting. Noah is alive. But will he ever stand on the ground again?

reflection_question: Is there a place in your life where you feel like God has forgotten you?
devotional_text:
Picture the inside of that ark. Day after day after day of water. No land anywhere. No other people anywhere. Just the sound of water against the wood, the noise of the animals, and eight people inside a boat that has been floating for months. On our last day the chapter ended with Noah alive but still surrounded. The waters prevailed a hundred and fifty days. The door was shut. And nothing outside had changed. If you were in that boat, what would you start to wonder? Has God forgotten about us? Is this how it ends? Are we just going to float forever? Then Genesis 8 opens with four words that turn the whole story around. And God remembered Noah. Not a new flood. Not another warning. God moves. And from this moment on, the water starts going the other way. But here is the thing. It does not all happen at once. The water goes down slowly. The boat stops, but the door stays shut. Mountain tops appear, but there is still no ground to stand on. God is bringing Noah out, but He is doing it in stages. Today we are reading Genesis 8:1–5.

G O D T U R N S T H E S T O R Y Genesis 8 begins with God doing something. “And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged;” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 Wait. God remembered Noah? Does that mean God forgot about him? Go all the way back to Day 1. We met a God who knows everything. Nothing slips past Him. He does not misplace people. He did not shut Noah inside that ark and then lose track of where He put him. So what does remembered mean here? In the Bible, when God remembers someone, it is not about recalling a fact He lost. It means God turns His attention to them and acts for them, because of a promise He made. You can see it in other places. When God destroyed the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, the Bible says God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out. Remembering meant rescuing. When Israel was crying out in slavery in Egypt, God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob, and then He moved to bring them out. That is what is happening here. God remembered Noah, and then God did something. And why would God act for Noah? Because He made a promise. Back before the rain ever fell, God said this: “But with thee will I establish my covenant; and thou shalt come into the ark, thou, and thy sons, and thy wife, and thy sons’ wives with thee.” G E N E S I S 6 : 1 8

Back on Day 15 we saw what a covenant is: a promise God binds Himself to. God did not bring Noah into the ark to leave him there. The same God who shut him in was always going to bring him out. Now look at who else God remembered. Every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark. God remembered the animals too. Not just the people. The goats and the birds and the creeping things. He had been keeping their seed alive on purpose. They mattered to Him then, and they still matter to Him now. Then God made a wind to pass over the earth. That is the first thing He does to start drying the world. The Hebrew word here is ruach. It can mean wind, breath, or spirit, depending on the sentence. In this verse it means wind. God sends a wind blowing across the water. But listen to how it sounds. Go back to Genesis 1:2: “And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.” G E N E S I S 1 : 2 At the very beginning, the earth was covered in water, and the Spirit of God moved over it. Then God made dry land appear. Now the earth is covered in water again, and a wind from God moves over it. The same God who made a world out of the water once is about to do it again. Genesis wants us to hear that echo. And then, the waters asswaged. Asswaged is an old word that means the waters went down. They settled. They started to sink. “The fountains also of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained;” G E N E S I S 8 : 2

Remember on our last day where the water came from. The fountains of the great deep from below and the windows of heaven from above. Now God closes both. The fountains are stopped. The windows are stopped. And the rain from heaven was restrained. That means held back. Like holding back a dog on a leash. The rain is not just running out. God is holding it back. Everything God opened in Genesis 7, He now shuts in Genesis 8. “And the waters returned from off the earth continually: and after the end of the hundred and fifty days the waters were abated.” G E N E S I S 8 : 3 Returned from off the earth continually means the water kept going back. Day after day. Steady. Not in one big drain. Slowly. Abated means lessened. The water level dropped. Now, here is something important for the timeline. The end of the hundred and fifty days. This is not a brand new hundred and fifty days starting now. It is the same hundred and fifty days we read about in Genesis 7:24. The waters prevailed for a hundred and fifty days from the start of the flood. At the end of that time, they began to go down. “And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat.” G E N E S I S 8 : 4 The ark stops moving. It rested. After months of floating, the bottom of that boat touches something solid.

Look at the date. Seventh month, seventeenth day. Now go back to when the flood started. Second month, seventeenth day. That is exactly five months later, to the day. Count those months at thirty days each, and you get a hundred and fifty days. The numbers line up. The day the waters finished prevailing is the day the ark came to rest. Where did it rest? Upon the mountains of Ararat. Notice it says mountains, plural. Ararat is the name of a region, not one single peak. It is a mountainous land that ancient records call Urartu, up in the high country where eastern Turkey and Armenia are today. Today there is a mountain called Mount Ararat in that area, and people have made all kinds of claims about finding the ark there. But the Bible does not point to one exact peak. It names the region, and that is what it wants us to know: the ark came to rest in the mountains. But here is something easy to miss. The ark resting is not the same as the earth being dry. The boat has stopped. But Noah still cannot get out. There is no ground to walk on. He is sitting on top of a mountain range that is still under water. The ark is still. But the waiting is not over. “And the waters decreased continually until the tenth month: in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, were the tops of the mountains seen.” G E N E S I S 8 : 5 Decreased continually. The water keeps going down. And then, in the tenth month, on the first day, the tops of the mountains appear. Think about how long that is. From the seventh month, seventeenth day, to the tenth month, first day. That is about two and a half more months. The ark had already been resting all that time before Noah could even see a mountain top.

Here is the timeline so far, all in one place: Look at how God is doing this. He does not snap His fingers and make the world dry in one second. First the fountains close. Then the rain stops. Then the water goes down. Then the ark rests. Then the mountain tops appear. Step by step. That should sound familiar. That is how God made the world in Genesis 1. Not all at once. Day by day. Light, then sky, then dry land, then plants, then life. God takes His time to prepare a world that people can live in. And here, after the flood, He is doing it again. Now think about this from inside the ark. Noah is not recorded hearing God explain each stage. As readers, we get to see what God is doing. We see the wind. We see the fountains stopped. We see the rain held back. But inside the boat, the family may have only felt the ark stop and seen the water still all around. That is a picture of what it is like to trust God when you cannot see everything. God was working the whole time. Even in the months when the only thing outside the window was water. This does not mean every hard thing in your life will end after a certain number of months. God did not promise that to you here. But it does show that a slow change is not the same as God forgetting. God remembered Noah, and from that moment on, every single day the water was a little lower. On the first day of the tenth month, for the first time in months, there was something to see besides water. Not dry ground yet. Not a way out yet. Just the tops of the mountains. But it was proof that the God who remembered was still at work. Second month, seventeenth day: the flood begins and the LORD shuts the door. ✦ The first forty days: rain falls and the ark is lifted up. ✦ Seventh month, seventeenth day: after a hundred and fifty days, the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat. ✦ Tenth month, first day: the tops of the mountains are seen. ✦

day_title: The Raven, the Dove, and the Wait
reflection_question: When you are waiting on God, do you lean more toward doing nothing or toward rushing ahead?
devotional_text:
Picture a window that has been shut for months. Behind it, eight people and a boat full of animals. Outside it, a world nobody in that boat has seen since the day God shut the door. They felt the ark come to rest on the mountains of Ararat. They know the mountain tops are showing now. But they still do not know what is out there. Is the ground dry? Is anything growing? Is there anywhere for a living thing to stand? Noah could have just sat there and waited for a voice from heaven. He could have kicked the door open the minute the boat stopped moving. He does neither. He opens the window. He sends out a bird. Then he watches, and he waits, and he sends out another one. That is what today is about. Waiting on God is not sitting still with your eyes closed. Noah waits, but he also pays attention. He takes small steps. He reads what is actually happening outside. And he does not let one good sign rush him into a conclusion it cannot carry. Noah waits with his eyes open. Today we are reading Genesis 8:6–12.

W A T C H I N G F O R S I G N S O F L I F E Yesterday we saw the turn of the whole flood story. God remembered Noah. God sent a wind. The water started going down. The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat in the seventh month, and in the tenth month, on the first day, the tops of the mountains could be seen. Now we pick up right there. “And it came to pass at the end of forty days, that Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made:” G E N E S I S 8 : 6 Be careful with that forty. It is not the whole voyage. It is not the forty days of rain either. This is forty days after the mountain tops started showing. The water is still going down, and Noah gives it time before he does anything. Then he opens the window of the ark which he had made. Go back to Genesis 6:16. God told Noah, A window shalt thou make to the ark. Noah built that window months, maybe years, before the rain. Now it becomes the way he looks out at a world that has been hidden from him. God gave Noah what he needed before he needed it. That window was part of the plan from the start. “And he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth.” G E N E S I S 8 : 7 The first bird out is a raven. A raven is a large black bird, a strong flier, the kind of bird that can stay out a long time and live off whatever it finds. Look at what it does. It went forth to and fro. That means back and forth. Out and around, again and again, until the waters were dried up.

People have built a lot of sermons on this raven. Some say it died. Some say it is a picture of an unbeliever who leaves God and never comes back. The verse does not say any of that. It says the raven went back and forth until the earth dried. That is all it tells us, so that is all we need to say. What we can say is this. The raven did not give Noah the clear answer he was looking for. So Noah tries again. “Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground;” G E N E S I S 8 : 8 Now the purpose is spelled out. He sends the dove to see if the waters were abated. Abated is the word we met yesterday. Gone down. Lessened. Noah is asking one practical question. Has the water pulled back from the ground yet? A dove is a different kind of bird than a raven. It is smaller and gentler, and it feeds on the ground. A dove needs a place to land. That is exactly why it makes a good test. “But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark, for the waters were on the face of the whole earth: then he put forth his hand, and took her, and pulled her in unto him into the ark.” G E N E S I S 8 : 9 First trip: nothing. No rest for the sole of her foot. Not one spot dry enough to land. But do not rush past the end of that verse. Then he put forth his hand, and took her, and pulled her in unto him into the ark. Slow down and see it. Noah leans out that window. He reaches out his hand. The tired little bird lands on it, and he pulls her back inside.

This is not a symbol on a greeting card. This is a man caring for a creature God put in his care. Back on Day 15, God told Noah to bring the animals into the ark to keep them alive. Noah is still doing that job. Even here, even while he is waiting on his own future, he is gentle with the life in his hands. And now he has his first piece of real news. The water is still too high. That is not the news anyone in that boat wanted. Imagine the family gathered around that window, watching the bird come back with nothing. It would be easy to get discouraged. It would be easy to say, we are never getting out of here. But bad news is still news. Noah now knows more than he knew this morning, and that helps him decide what to do next. So what does he do next? He waits. “And he stayed yet other seven days; and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark;” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 0 Stayed here means waited. Noah waited seven more days. And notice the word other. Yet other seven days. That little word suggests he had already waited seven days before. Noah is living in weeks now. Wait seven days. Try again. Wait seven days. Try again. Think about how long a week feels when you are stuck inside a boat that smells like a barn. Noah does not force it. He gives it the time it needs. And remember who has been in that boat the whole time. Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives. They have been inside since the second month of Noah’s six hundredth year. By now it has been many months. Every seven day wait is one more week of feeding animals, cleaning stalls and wondering. Waiting is real work.

“And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth.” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 1 Second trip: the dove is gone all day. She comes back in the evening. And there in her beak is an olive leaf, pluckt off. That means freshly picked, torn right off a living tree. Why does that matter so much? Because a fresh leaf is information. It means something is growing out there again. It means the water has gone down far enough for a bird to reach a tree and pick from it. It means life is coming back. Picture Noah holding that one little leaf. Think back to Day 2, when God made dry land appear and told the earth to bring forth grass and trees yielding fruit. Then think about everything the flood just wiped away. And now here is one green leaf, proof that the world God made is starting to breathe again. One more thing. Most paintings show the dove carrying a long olive branch. The Bible says a leaf. One leaf. God does not need a big sign to say a lot. Look at what the verse says next: so Noah knew. Noah came to know something, one step at a time. But look at what he knew. He knew the waters had gone down. He did not decide every field was ready. He did not open the door that night. One leaf is a good sign, but it is not the whole answer. “And he stayed yet other seven days; and sent forth the dove; which returned not again unto him any more.” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 2 Third trip: she does not come back at all.

That silence is the news. The dove found somewhere to rest and something to eat. She could live out there now. And still, Noah does not walk out. He waits for God to tell him to go. That happens in our next reading. Now step back and look at the whole thing. Three trips. Three answers. The evidence grows over time. Noah takes every stage seriously. He does not ignore the bad news, and he does not overreact to the good news. He waits, he watches, and he takes the next small step. Some people think faith means you shut your eyes and do nothing until heaven speaks. Other people think faith means you grab the first good sign and run. Noah shows us neither one is right. He opened the window. He sent the birds. He paid attention. And he still left the final word to God. Prayer and practical steps belong together. This is not a method for reading birds or signs in the sky. It is a picture of a man who trusts God and still uses the eyes and hands God gave him. A dove shows up again later in the Bible. When Jesus was baptized in Matthew 3:16, he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove. And many people today use an olive leaf as a picture of peace. Those are good connections to enjoy, but Genesis 8 is not telling us this dove is the Holy Spirit. Here the dove has a job. She tells Noah what is happening outside the ark. So what is happening outside the ark? The waters are going down. Things are growing. A bird has found a home. The God who sent the flood is bringing the world back to life. And the dove that did not come back is the quiet signal that Noah and his family are getting close to the door. No resting place. The water is still too high. ✦ A fresh olive leaf. Life is growing again. ✦ No return. A bird can live out there now. ✦

reflection_question: Is there a place where you can see dry ground but have not heard God say go?
devotional_text:
The dove did not come back. Noah has been watching that window for weeks. First the dove came back with nothing. Then she came back with a fresh olive leaf. Then she flew off and never returned. Out there, somewhere, a bird has found a place to live. So why is Noah still inside? Because a bird finding a home is not the same thing as God saying go. Think about how this whole journey started. Noah did not walk into the ark because the clouds looked dark. He walked in because God told him to come in. And the Bible says the LORD shut him in. Noah did not close that door. God did. Now the question is, who opens it? Today the signs give way to something better. God speaks again. The same God who said come in now says go out. And when Noah and his family finally step onto that ground, they are not stepping into a finished world. They are stepping into a world that needs to be lived in and built up again. Rescue brings them out. It does not end their work. Today we are reading Genesis 8:13–19.

T H E S A M E G O D S A Y S G O Genesis slows down here and gives us dates. Pay attention to them, because they show us just how long this family was inside that boat. “And it came to pass in the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried up from off the earth: and Noah removed the covering of the ark, and looked, and, behold, the face of the ground was dry.” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 3 The six hundredth and first year means the year of Noah’s life. His six hundredth year is over, and a new one has begun. First month. First day. It is literally New Year’s Day on Noah’s calendar, and the water is gone from the surface of the earth. So Noah does something new. He removed the covering of the ark. The covering is the top of the boat, the roof that kept them sheltered all those months. Up to now he has been looking through a window. Now he opens the top and gets a real look. And what does he see? The face of the ground was dry. That is huge. But look at the next verse. “And in the second month, on the seven and twentieth day of the month, was the earth dried.” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 4 Second month. Twenty seventh day. Almost two more months go by.

Why? Because there is a difference between the top of the ground looking dry and the earth being ready to live on. You have seen this after a big rain. The surface looks fine, but step on it and your foot sinks into mud. This land had been under water for months. Genesis shows it drying in stages, from the surface being dry to the whole earth being dried. Noah is not being lazy or slow here. He is not doubting God. He is waiting for the ground to be ready, and he is waiting for God to speak. Think about what that wait would feel like. You have been inside for most of a year. You pull back the covering and see dry ground with your own eyes. Everything in you wants to climb down and run. And then you wait almost two more months. That takes trust. Noah is trusting that God knows when the ground is ready better than he does. He has watched God be faithful for a whole year. He is not going to stop trusting Him now, right at the finish line. Now let us put the whole timeline in one place, because these last few days have been full of numbers. Go back to Genesis 7:11. The flood began in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month. Now in Genesis 8:14 the earth is dried in the second month, on the seven and twentieth day, one year later. So by the dates Genesis gives, this family was in the ark a little more than a full year. That surprises a lot of people. We hear forty days and forty nights and think the whole flood lasted about a month. But the forty days was just the rain. Here is the order, step by step: The flood begins: Noah’s six hundredth year, second month, seventeenth day. ✦ Rain falls forty days and forty nights. ✦ The waters prevail upon the earth a hundred and fifty days. ✦ The ark rests on the mountains of Ararat: seventh month, seventeenth day. ✦

One more thing about that list. Remember from Day 17, the forty days of rain sit inside the hundred and fifty days, not on top of them. So you cannot just add all the numbers together. Follow the dates, and the dates tell you it was about a year. A whole year. Think about that. Every day, feeding animals. Every day, cleaning up after them. Every day, the same eight faces. A whole year of trusting God inside a boat. And then, finally: “And God spake unto Noah, saying,” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 5 That is the moment. Not the raven. Not the olive leaf. Not the dry ground. God spake unto Noah. Here is the lesson in that. Noah used his eyes. He opened the window. He sent the birds. He removed the covering and looked. Faith and paying attention go together. But when it came to leaving the ark, Noah waited for God’s word, because God was the One who brought him in. Remember Genesis 7:1. Come thou and all thy house into the ark. And Genesis 7:16 told us the LORD shut him in. God opened this chapter of Noah’s life. So God gets to close it. The tops of the mountains are seen: tenth month, first day. ✦ Forty days later, Noah opens the window and sends the raven and the dove. ✦ The ground is dry and Noah removes the covering: six hundred and first year, first month, first day. ✦ The earth is dried: second month, twenty seventh day. ✦ God tells Noah to go out. ✦

“Go forth of the ark, thou, and thy wife, and thy sons, and thy sons’ wives with thee.” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 6 Go forth simply means go out. And look at who God names. Noah. His wife. His sons. His sons’ wives. It is the same family list from Genesis 6:18, when God first told Noah who would come into the ark. Every one of them went in. Every one of them is coming out. God did not lose a single person He promised to keep. Then God turns to the animals: “Bring forth with thee every living thing that is with thee, of all flesh, both of fowl, and of cattle, and of every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth; that they may breed abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply upon the earth.” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 7 Listen to that last part. Be fruitful, and multiply. Where have we heard that before? Day 3. Genesis 1:22. When God made the fish and the birds, He blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply. Now, after the flood, God says it again. Breed abundantly means have lots of young. Fill the earth back up. This is why the animals were saved in the first place. Back in Genesis 6:19, God told Noah to bring them in to keep them alive. The ark was never meant to be a zoo that floats forever. It was a way to carry life through the judgment so it could start over on the other side. Remember what we saw back on Day 2. God builds systems. Day and night. Seasons. Seeds inside the fruit. Animals that bring forth young after their kind. The flood did not erase God’s design. In a changed world, the same God starts the same rhythms of life all over again.

“And Noah went forth, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons’ wives with him:” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 8 Simple. God said go. Noah went. Notice the verse does not say Noah argued, or asked for one more week, or sent out one more bird to be sure. The birds gave him information. God’s word gave him direction. When the direction came, he did not need anything else. That has been Noah’s pattern this whole story. When God said build, he built. When God said come in, he came in. When God said go out, he went out. Back on Day 15 we read Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he. That never changed. This does not mean safe places are bad, or that God always wants you to leave where you are. Staying in the ark was obedience. Leaving the ark was obedience. The point is not stay or go. The point is listening to God and moving when He moves. “Every beast, every creeping thing, and every fowl, and whatsoever creepeth upon the earth, after their kinds, went forth out of the ark.” G E N E S I S 8 : 1 9 Then come the animals. After their kinds means by their families, each group with its own kind. They did not come out in one wild stampede. They went out group by group, the way they had come in. Now try to picture that first step. The ground under their feet is soft and new. The air is quiet. There are no roads, no houses, no neighbors, no fields already planted. The world they knew before is gone. You do not need a lot of imagination to see that the work ahead of them was enormous.

Rescue got them through the flood. It did not hand them a finished life. Now they would have to plant, build, raise families and learn how to live in this world. That is how God often works with us too. He carries us through the thing that should have ended us. Then He opens the door and says go out and live. The ark was where God kept them. The open ground is where God sends them. And before they build anything else, Noah is about to build something for God.

day_title: An Altar and a New Beginning
reflection_question: When God brings you through something hard, what is the first thing you do?
devotional_text:
The door is open. The animals are spreading out across the hills. Noah and his family are standing on dry ground for the first time in a year. So what is the first thing he does? He does not build a house. The Bible does not show him planting a field first, or exploring the land, or making plans. The first thing Genesis records Noah doing outside that ark is building an altar to God. Think about everything that led to this moment. Twenty days ago we started at the very beginning, with God creating a world He called very good. Then we watched it fall apart. One bite of forbidden fruit. Then hiding. Then blame. Then a brother killed in a field. Then violence filling the whole earth, until God judged it with a flood. And through all of it, God kept one family alive. Now that family stands in a washed out world, and before anything else, they worship. Today we will see how God answers that worship. We will hear what God says in His heart about people, about the ground, and about the future. And we will see that the God who made the seasons on the first pages of Genesis is still keeping them running. The world starts over at an altar.

W O R S H I P A T T H E S T A R T O F A N E W W O R L D “And Noah builded an altar unto the LORD; and took of every clean beast, and of every clean fowl, and offered burnt offerings on the altar.” G E N E S I S 8 : 2 0 This is the first time the word altar shows up in the Bible. An altar is a place built for presenting offerings to God. What matters most is who it was for. Unto the LORD. Then look at what Noah offers. Every clean beast and every clean fowl. Go back to Day 16. In Genesis 7:2, God told Noah, Of every clean beast thou shalt take to thee by sevens. Of the animals that were not clean, Noah took two. But the clean animals and birds came in by sevens. Now we see what Day 16 pointed to. God provided extra so there would be something to give back to Him. Before the flood even started, God was already making room for worship on the other side of it. But do not miss how costly this is. These are not animals from a big farm with thousands more in the barn. These are some of the only animals left on the entire earth. Every one of them could have been food, or wool, or the start of a new herd. Noah takes from that small number and gives it to God. That is real worship. It is not giving God whatever is left over. It is giving Him something that costs you. Remember Cain and Abel on Day 10. Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering. Abel brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. God had respect unto Abel’s offering, but not Cain’s. Hebrews 11:4 tells us by faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain. It was never just about the animal. It was about a heart that trusted God and gave Him the best.

Noah is standing in that same line. Hebrews 11:7 says by faith Noah prepared the ark. Now by faith Noah worships. What kind of offering is it? Burnt offerings. That means the whole animal was burned up on the altar and given to God. Nothing was kept back. Much later, in the book of Leviticus, God gave Israel detailed rules about the burnt offering. Leviticus 1:9 calls it an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD. In that later teaching, the burnt offering is a picture of giving yourself completely to God and being accepted by Him. Those rules had not been given yet in Noah’s day, but they help us see what this kind of offering meant. Noah is holding nothing back. And why does he do it? The Bible does not record a prayer or a speech. But you do not need words to read this. A man who just survived the end of the world, whose whole family is alive, does not need to be told to say thank You. He is grateful. And he knows he did not save himself. “And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake; for the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done.” G E N E S I S 8 : 2 1 The LORD smelled a sweet savour. Savour is an old word for a smell or an aroma. A sweet savour is a pleasing smell. Now be careful here. God is not hungry. He does not need smoke from a fire. He cannot be bribed into being good. This is the Bible’s way of telling us God was pleased. He accepted Noah’s offering, the same way He accepted Abel’s. What pleased God was not the smoke. It was a man coming to Him in faith with a grateful heart.

Next, notice who God is talking to. The LORD said in his heart. That means this is God’s own resolve, what He decided within Himself. Genesis is letting us hear it. It is not a new speech out loud to Noah. We get to listen in on the heart of God. And what is in God’s heart? I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake. Go back to Day 9. After Adam sinned, God said cursed is the ground for thy sake. Thorns. Thistles. Hard work. That has not disappeared. People still sweat in the fields. Weeds still grow. People still die. So what is God promising? Look at the end of the verse. Neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done. God is promising He will not do this again. He will not wipe out all life on the earth like He did in the flood. Now here comes the part that surprises people. Look at the reason God gives. For the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth. Wait. Is that not the same problem that caused the flood? It is. Go back to Day 14. Genesis 6:5 said every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. That is why God sent the flood. Now, after the flood, God says the same thing. The human heart is still bent toward evil, and it starts young. That means the flood did not fix people. It washed away a violent world, but it did not wash the sin out of the human heart. Noah’s family walked off that boat with the same problem Adam had. God knows that. And instead of saying, so I will destroy them again, God says, I will not do this again. That is patience. That is mercy. God is choosing to keep the world going and to let history continue, knowing exactly what people are like. He is going to keep working His plan inside a world full of people who need Him.

That is why the rest of the Bible exists. People do not get better on their own. The answer to the human heart was never going to be another flood. It was going to be God Himself, working through history, all the way to Jesus. “While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.” G E N E S I S 8 : 2 2 This is the last verse of our book, and it is a beautiful one. While the earth remaineth means for as long as the earth is still here. And look at the four pairs: Seedtime simply means planting season. Shall not cease means it will not stop. As long as the earth remains, these rhythms keep going. This does not mean every place has the same weather, or that every farmer is promised a good crop every year. Droughts still happen. Storms still come. It means the big cycles that keep life going will not be shut off again like they were in the flood. And this brings us right back to the beginning. On Day 2 and Day 3 we saw something about God that runs through this whole book. God creates systems. He did not just make things. He made rhythms that keep things going. Day and night. Seasons. Seeds inside the fruit, so plants make more plants. Genesis 1:14 says God made the lights in the sky to be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years. The flood interrupted all of that. Now God says it is back, and it will keep running. Seedtime and harvest: a time to plant and a time to gather. ✦ Cold and heat. ✦ Summer and winter. ✦ Day and night. ✦

Think about what that means for your life. Every morning the sun comes up. Every spring something gets planted. Every harvest something gets gathered. Every one of those is God keeping His word from Genesis 8:22. Every sunrise is another day of opportunity He has given the world. So step back and look at the whole road we have walked. We started with God alone, creating the heavens and the earth. We watched Him bring order out of darkness and fill the world with life. We watched Him make man and woman in His image and call everything very good. Then we watched it break. A fruit. A lie. A hiding place. A murder. A man named Lamech bragging about killing. And a world so full of violence that God was grieved at His heart. Then we watched God judge it. But we also watched Him save. One man found grace. One ark. One family. One window. One dove. One altar. That is the story of the beginning of everything. God judges sin, and God preserves life. He does not give up on the world He made. This promise in Genesis 8 is not the end of God’s commitment to Noah. Back in Genesis 6:18 God already told Noah, with thee will I establish my covenant. In the chapter that comes next, God speaks to Noah’s family directly and gives them a sign to remember it by. That is where our next volume, The Obedience of Abraham, begins. It opens with Genesis 9 and follows Noah’s family as they spread out into nations, build a tower at Babel, and eventually lead to one man God calls by name. His name is Abram. But for now, stand with Noah at that altar. Smell the smoke going up. Feel the quiet of a brand new world. People are not perfect. Their hearts are still the same. But God has given humanity a future, and it starts with worship.
